title: Palletize a pinwheel layer
instruction: Put one carton in each corner of the pallet, lying flat on its largest face and square to the pallet, with its two outer sides flush with the pallet's edges.
context: Hand palletizers build each layer to a pattern so the cartons fill the pallet edge to edge and the load stays square. When a carton's length plus its width just fits the pallet side, the layer is a pinwheel: two cartons along one edge don't fit, so two of the four have to be turned 90 degrees. Done by: laborers and freight, stock, and material movers.
setup: The two arm bases stand 61 cm apart on an oak table. Four identical corrugated cartons (100 x 50 x 40 mm, 150 g) lie flat on a 100 x 50 mm face, their 100 mm sides pointing straight out from the arms: two in front of each arm, centred 5.5 cm in from that arm's base toward the midline, at 18 and 33 cm out. A blue plastic pallet (170 x 170 mm, 20 mm tall) is fixed to the table on the midline between the arms, its centre 30 cm out, its edges square to the table.
scoring: A carton fills a pallet corner when it lies flat on its largest (100 x 50 mm) face, resting on the pallet itself and not on another carton or held above it (its 40 mm side within 5 degrees of vertical), its sides within 5 degrees of square to the pallet's edges, and each of its two outer sides between 3 mm past and 15 mm inside the pallet's edge at that corner. 0.25 for each filled corner. 1.0 when all four corners are filled and every carton is still for 1 s, which ends the trial; four filled at the last step also scores 1.0. Two cartons along one edge overlap by at least 24 mm, so four filled corners are only possible as a pinwheel, either way round.
reset_notes: Lay the cartons back, two in front of each arm, their 100 mm sides pointing away from the arms.
fidelity: Cartons are filled, rigid 150 g boxes with sharp edges: no flaps, no give. The pallet is a solid square block fixed to the table. Its side is a carton's length plus its width plus 20 mm of play, so the fingers fit between cartons; real layers are tight. Every object has the same rubber-like friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic), more than cardboard on plastic.
